# cidr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cidr/

## Expand description

This library provides types to represent an IP network ([ Cidr](https://docs.rs/trait.Cidr.html)) or
an IP host withing a network (

[)](https://docs.rs/trait.Inet.html)

`Inet`The naming follows the names of the [PostgreSQL data types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/static/datatype-net-types.html)

By default address parsing is done using `FromStr` from the standard
library, which is rather strict in the inputs it accepts.
[ Cidr](https://docs.rs/trait.Cidr.html) types don’t accept addresses with host-bits set (i.e.

`127.0.0.1/8`
isn’t valid; it should be `127.0.0.0/8`).Custom parsing can be implemented using the helpers in the [ parsers](https://docs.rs/parsers/index.html) module.

If the `#` flag is used with the `Display` formatting (i.e. `{:#}`) the
prefix length will be shown even for host addresses (added in `0.1.1`).

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-no_unsafe)Feature `no_unsafe`

Enables `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` for the whole crate; needs to use
some workarounds that are likely slower than their `unsafe` variants.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-std)Feature `std`

Enabled by default, currently unused.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-serde)Feature `serde`

This feature enables various types to be serialized using `serde`
(without `serde-derive`).

In human readable formats the `Display` and `FromStr` interfaces are
used.  Otherwise all values are serialized in the same format (apart
from the newtype wrapping) as a tuple of two values:

- `tag: u8`:- `0x00...0x20`: IPv4 with network length- `tag`
- `0x40...0xc0`: IPv6 with network length- `tag - 0x40`
- `0xff`:- `any`

- address according to `tag`:`Ipv4Addr``[u8; 4]`),`Ipv6Addr``[u8; 16]`) or`()`

The represenation hasn’t been changed in 0.2; it is compatible with 0.1.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-bitstring)Feature `bitstring`

This feature allows various types to be used as [ bitstring::BitString](https://docs.rs/bitstring/0.2.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/bitstring/bit_string/trait.BitString.html),
which allows them being in used in containers like

[bitstring-trees](https://crates.io/crates/bitstring-trees).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Inet](https://docs.rs/struct.InetAddressIterator.html)- Address - Iterator
- Iterator type to iterate over a list of IP addresses in a network
- [Inet](https://docs.rs/struct.InetIterator.html)- Iterator
- Iterator type to iterate over a list of IP addresses within a network
- [Ipv4](https://docs.rs/struct.Ipv4Cidr.html)- Cidr
- `Cidr`
- [Ipv4](https://docs.rs/struct.Ipv4Inet.html)- Inet
- `Inet`
- [Ipv4](https://docs.rs/struct.Ipv4InetPair.html)- Inet - Pair
- `InetPair`
- [Ipv6](https://docs.rs/struct.Ipv6Cidr.html)- Cidr
- `Cidr`
- [Ipv6](https://docs.rs/struct.Ipv6Inet.html)- Inet
- `Inet`
- [Ipv6](https://docs.rs/struct.Ipv6InetPair.html)- Inet - Pair
- `InetPair`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [AnyIp](https://docs.rs/enum.AnyIpCidr.html)- Cidr
- Represents either an IPv4 or an IPv6 network or “any”.
- [Family](https://docs.rs/enum.Family.html)
- Represents the type of an IP address
- [IpCidr](https://docs.rs/enum.IpCidr.html)
- `Cidr`
- [IpInet](https://docs.rs/enum.IpInet.html)
- `Inet`
- [IpInet](https://docs.rs/enum.IpInetPair.html)- Pair
- `InetPair`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Address](https://docs.rs/trait.Address.html)
- Maps IP address type to other types based on this address type
- [Cidr](https://docs.rs/trait.Cidr.html)
- Types implementing `Cidr``network_length`.
- [Inet](https://docs.rs/trait.Inet.html)
- Types implementing Inet represent IP hosts within networks.
- [Inet](https://docs.rs/trait.InetPair.html)- Pair
- Pair of two addresses in the same network

# cidr 0.3.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cidr/latest

# cidr crate

This library provides types to represent an IP network (`Cidr`) or an IP
host within a network (`Inet`).

The naming follows the names of the [PostgreSQL data types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/static/datatype-net-types.html)

The documentation for `master` is located at [https://stbuehler.github.io/rustdocs/cidr/cidr/](https://stbuehler.github.io/rustdocs/cidr/cidr/); released versions are documented at [https://docs.rs/cidr](https://docs.rs/cidr).

## Examples

- example making good use of the `bitstring`feature and the`bitstring-trees`crate:[https://github.com/stbuehler/rust-gather-cidr-map](https://github.com/stbuehler/rust-gather-cidr-map)

# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0.210/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [forward_](https://docs.rs/macro.forward_to_deserialize_any.html)- to_ - deserialize_ - any - `docsrs`
- Helper macro when implementing the `Deserializer`part of a new data format for Serde.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Deserialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Serialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.

# bincode - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bincode/^1.3.1/

## Expand description

Bincode is a crate for encoding and decoding using a tiny binary serialization strategy. Using it, you can easily go from having an object in memory, quickly serialize it to bytes, and then deserialize it back just as fast!

[§](https://docs.rs#using-basic-functions)Using Basic Functions

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fn main() {
    // The object that we will serialize.
    let target: Option<String>  = Some("hello world".to_string());
    let encoded: Vec<u8> = bincode::serialize(&target).unwrap();
    let decoded: Option<String> = bincode::deserialize(&encoded[..]).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(target, decoded);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#128bit-numbers)128bit numbers

Support for `i128` and `u128` is automatically enabled on Rust toolchains
greater than or equal to `1.26.0` and disabled for targets which do not support it

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use config::`- [Config](https://docs.rs/config/struct.Config.html);- Deprecated
- `pub use config::`- [DefaultOptions](https://docs.rs/config/struct.DefaultOptions.html);
- `pub use config::`- [Options](https://docs.rs/config/trait.Options.html);
- `pub use de::read::`- [BincodeRead](https://docs.rs/de/read/trait.BincodeRead.html);
- `pub use de::`- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/de/struct.Deserializer.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [config](https://docs.rs/config/index.html)
- `bincode`uses a Builder-pattern to configure the Serializers and Deserializers in this crate. This means that if you need to customize the behavior of- `bincode`, you should create an instance of the- `DefaultOptions`struct:
- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Deserialize bincode data to a Rust data structure.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/struct.Serializer.html)
- An Serializer that encodes values directly into a Writer.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.ErrorKind.html)- Kind
- The kind of error that can be produced during a serialization or deserialization.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [config](https://docs.rs/fn.config.html)- Deprecated
- Get a default configuration object.
- [deserialize](https://docs.rs/fn.deserialize.html)
- Deserializes a slice of bytes into an instance of `T`using the default configuration.
- [deserialize_](https://docs.rs/fn.deserialize_from.html)- from
- Deserializes an object directly from a `Read`er using the default configuration.
- [deserialize_](https://docs.rs/fn.deserialize_from_custom.html)- from_ - custom
- Deserializes an object from a custom `BincodeRead`er using the default configuration. It is highly recommended to use`deserialize_from`unless you need to implement`BincodeRead`for performance reasons.
- [options](https://docs.rs/fn.options.html)
- Get a default configuration object.
- [serialize](https://docs.rs/fn.serialize.html)
- Serializes a serializable object into a `Vec`of bytes using the default configuration.
- [serialize_](https://docs.rs/fn.serialize_into.html)- into
- Serializes an object directly into a `Writer`using the default configuration.
- [serialized_](https://docs.rs/fn.serialized_size.html)- size
- Returns the size that an object would be if serialized using Bincode with the default configuration.

# serde_test - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_test/^1.0.27/

## Expand description

This crate provides a convenient concise way to write unit tests for
implementations of [ Serialize](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/ser/trait.Serialize.html) and

[.](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/de/trait.Deserialize.html)

`Deserialize`The `Serialize` impl for a value can be characterized by the sequence of
[ Serializer](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/ser/trait.Serializer.html) calls that are made in the course of serializing the value,
so

`serde_test` provides a [abstraction which corresponds roughly to](https://docs.rs/enum.Token.html)

`Token``Serializer` method calls. There is an [function to test that a value serializes to a particular sequence of method calls, an](https://docs.rs/fn.assert_ser_tokens.html)

`assert_ser_tokens`[function to test that a value can be deserialized from a particular sequence of method calls, and an](https://docs.rs/fn.assert_de_tokens.html)

`assert_de_tokens`[function to test both directions. There are also functions to test expected failure conditions.](https://docs.rs/fn.assert_tokens.html)

`assert_tokens`Here is an example from the [ linked-hash-map](https://github.com/contain-rs/linked-hash-map) crate.

```
use linked_hash_map::LinkedHashMap;
use serde_test::{assert_tokens, Token};
#[test]
fn test_ser_de_empty() {
    let map = LinkedHashMap::<char, u32>::new();
    assert_tokens(
        &map,
        &[
            Token::Map { len: Some(0) },
            Token::MapEnd,
        ],
    );
}
#[test]
fn test_ser_de() {
    let mut map = LinkedHashMap::new();
    map.insert('b', 20);
    map.insert('a', 10);
    map.insert('c', 30);
    assert_tokens(
        &map,
        &[
            Token::Map { len: Some(3) },
            Token::Char('b'),
            Token::I32(20),
            Token::Char('a'),
            Token::I32(10),
            Token::Char('c'),
            Token::I32(30),
            Token::MapEnd,
        ],
    );
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Configure](https://docs.rs/trait.Configure.html)
- Trait to determine whether a value is represented in human-readable or compact form.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [assert_](https://docs.rs/fn.assert_de_tokens.html)- de_ - tokens
- Asserts that the given `tokens`deserialize into`value`.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/fn.assert_de_tokens_error.html)- de_ - tokens_ - error
- Asserts that the given `tokens`yield`error`when deserializing.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/fn.assert_ser_tokens.html)- ser_ - tokens
- Asserts that `value`serializes to the given`tokens`.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/fn.assert_ser_tokens_error.html)- ser_ - tokens_ - error
- Asserts that `value`serializes to the given`tokens`, and then yields`error`.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/fn.assert_tokens.html)- tokens
- Runs both `assert_ser_tokens`and`assert_de_tokens`.

# version_sync - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/version-sync/^0.9.1/

## Expand description

`version-sync` provides macros for keeping version numbers in sync
with your crate version.

[§](https://docs.rs#library-overview)Library Overview

When making a release of a Rust project, you typically need to adjust some version numbers in your code and documentation. This crate gives you macros that covers some typical cases where version numbers need updating:

-
TOML examples in the `README.md`files that show how to add a dependency on your crate. See`assert_markdown_deps_updated`
-
A `Changelog.md`file that should at least mention the current version. See`assert_contains_regex``assert_contains_substring`
-
A `README.md`file which should only mention the current version. See`assert_only_contains_regex`
-
The `html_root_url``assert_html_root_url_updated`

Except for [ assert_contains_substring](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_contains_substring.html), the macros are gated
behind individual features, as detailed below.

A typical configuration will use an integration test to verify
that all version numbers are in sync. Create a
`tests/version-numbers.rs` file with:

```
#[test]
fn test_readme_deps_updated() {
    version_sync::assert_markdown_deps_updated!("README.md");
}
#[test]
fn test_readme_mentions_version() {
    version_sync::assert_contains_substring!("README.md", "Version {version}");
}
#[test]
fn test_html_root_url() {
    version_sync::assert_html_root_url_updated!("src/lib.rs");
}
```
When you run `cargo test`, your version numbers will be
automatically checked.

[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo Features

In case you only need some of the macros above, you can disable them individually using Cargo features. The features are:

- `markdown_deps_updated`enables- `assert_markdown_deps_updated`
- `html_root_url_updated`enables- `assert_html_root_url_updated`
- `contains_regex`enables- `assert_contains_regex`- `assert_only_contains_regex`

All of these features are enabled by default. If you disable all
of them, you can still use [ assert_contains_substring](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_contains_substring.html) to
quickly check that a given file contains the current crate
version.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_contains_regex.html)- contains_ - regex
- Assert that versions numbers are up to date via a regex.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_contains_substring.html)- contains_ - substring
- Assert that versions numbers are up to date via substring matching.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_html_root_url_updated.html)- html_ - root_ - url_ - updated
- Assert that the `html_root_url`attribute is up to date.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_markdown_deps_updated.html)- markdown_ - deps_ - updated
- Assert that dependencies on the current package are up to date.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_only_contains_regex.html)- only_ - contains_ - regex
- Assert that all versions numbers are up to date via a regex.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_contains_regex.html)- contains_ - regex
- Check that `path`contain the regular expression given by`template`.
- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_contains_substring.html)- contains_ - substring
- Check that `path`contain the substring given by`template`.
- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_html_root_url.html)- html_ - root_ - url
- Check version numbers in `html_root_url`attributes.
- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_markdown_deps.html)- markdown_ - deps
- Check dependencies in Markdown code blocks.
- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_only_contains_regex.html)- only_ - contains_ - regex
- Check that `path`only contains matches to the regular expression given by`template`.

# cidr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cidr/latest/target-redirect/cidr/

## Expand description

This library provides types to represent an IP network ([ Cidr](https://docs.rs/trait.Cidr.html)) or
an IP host withing a network (

[)](https://docs.rs/trait.Inet.html)

`Inet`The naming follows the names of the [PostgreSQL data types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/static/datatype-net-types.html)

By default address parsing is done using `FromStr` from the standard
library, which is rather strict in the inputs it accepts.
[ Cidr](https://docs.rs/trait.Cidr.html) types don’t accept addresses with host-bits set (i.e.

`127.0.0.1/8`
isn’t valid; it should be `127.0.0.0/8`).Custom parsing can be implemented using the helpers in the [ parsers](https://docs.rs/parsers/index.html) module.

If the `#` flag is used with the `Display` formatting (i.e. `{:#}`) the
prefix length will be shown even for host addresses (added in `0.1.1`).

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-no_unsafe)Feature `no_unsafe`

Enables `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` for the whole crate; needs to use
some workarounds that are likely slower than their `unsafe` variants.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-std)Feature `std`

Enabled by default, currently unused.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-serde)Feature `serde`

This feature enables various types to be serialized using `serde`
(without `serde-derive`).

In human readable formats the `Display` and `FromStr` interfaces are
used.  Otherwise all values are serialized in the same format (apart
from the newtype wrapping) as a tuple of two values:

- `tag: u8`:- `0x00...0x20`: IPv4 with network length- `tag`
- `0x40...0xc0`: IPv6 with network length- `tag - 0x40`
- `0xff`:- `any`

- address according to `tag`:`Ipv4Addr``[u8; 4]`),`Ipv6Addr``[u8; 16]`) or`()`

The represenation hasn’t been changed in 0.2; it is compatible with 0.1.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-bitstring)Feature `bitstring`

This feature allows various types to be used as [ bitstring::BitString](https://docs.rs/bitstring/0.2.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/bitstring/bit_string/trait.BitString.html),
which allows them being in used in containers like

[bitstring-trees](https://crates.io/crates/bitstring-trees).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Inet](https://docs.rs/struct.InetAddressIterator.html)- Address - Iterator
- Iterator type to iterate over a list of IP addresses in a network
- [Inet](https://docs.rs/struct.InetIterator.html)- Iterator
- Iterator type to iterate over a list of IP addresses within a network

- `Cidr`
- [Ipv6](https://docs.rs/struct.Ipv6Inet.html)- Inet

- Represents either an IPv4 or an IPv6 network or “any”.

- Represents the type of an IP address

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

Source: https://docs.rs/about/badges

Docs.rs no longer has its own badges. Consider using [shields.io](https://shields.io) instead.

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# smooth_operator_adapter_memory - Rust

## Expand description

In-memory [ StorageAdapter](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator/1.11.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator/adapter/trait.StorageAdapter.html) — the conformance / test baseline.

All OLTP slices (conversations, participants, messages, sessions) live in
`HashMap`s behind a single `RwLock`. The checkpoint and knowledge slices
delegate to smooth-operator’s own [ MemoryCheckpointStore](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-core/0.15.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator_core/checkpoint/struct.MemoryCheckpointStore.html) and

[, which are exactly what the engine expects — so this adapter is a faithful (if non-durable) stand-in for Postgres/DynamoDB.](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-core/0.15.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator_core/knowledge/struct.InMemoryKnowledge.html)

# smooth_operator_ingestion - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-ingestion/1.11.1/smooth_operator_ingestion/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#smooth-operator-ingestion)smooth-operator ingestion

Knowledge **ingestion + connectors** for smooth-operator — the pipeline
that pulls documents from a source, chunks them, embeds them, and stores them
in the [ StorageAdapter](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator/1.11.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator/adapter/trait.StorageAdapter.html)
knowledge slice so they are retrievable. This closes feature gap G1 (knowledge
ingestion + connectors), G2 (document chunking pipeline), and G9 (the
connector mock +

`unit`-vs-`external` test split). See `docs/INGESTION.md`.[§](https://docs.rs#shape)Shape

```
Connector::pull ─▶ Chunker::chunk ─▶ Embedder::embed ─▶ KnowledgeBase::ingest
   RawDocument        Vec<Chunk>        Vec<Vec<f32>>        (StorageAdapter
                                                              knowledge slice)
```
- `Connector`- `RawDocument`- `pull(since)`). Built-ins:- `FileConnector`- `WebConnector`- `MockConnector`
- `Chunker`
- `Embedder`- `smooth_operator::embedding`- `DeterministicEmbedder`
- `ingest`- `(doc id, content hash)`via an- `IngestLedger`

[§](https://docs.rs#wiring-example)Wiring example

```
let connector = FileConnector::new("./docs");
let report = ingest(
    &connector,
    &Chunker::default(),
    &DeterministicEmbedder::new(),
    storage.knowledge(),
    IngestOptions::for_org("org-acme"),
)
.await?;
println!("stored {} chunks", report.chunks_stored);
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use chunker::`- [Chunk](https://docs.rs/chunker/struct.Chunk.html);
- `pub use chunker::`- [Chunker](https://docs.rs/chunker/struct.Chunker.html);
- `pub use chunker::`- [DEFAULT_MAX_CHARS](https://docs.rs/chunker/constant.DEFAULT_MAX_CHARS.html);
- `pub use chunker::`- [DEFAULT_OVERLAP_CHARS](https://docs.rs/chunker/constant.DEFAULT_OVERLAP_CHARS.html);
- `pub use connector::`- [Connector](https://docs.rs/connector/trait.Connector.html);
- `pub use connector::`- [MockConnector](https://docs.rs/connector/struct.MockConnector.html);

- Document → chunks (feature gap G2).

- The `Connector`
- [connectors](https://docs.rs/connectors/index.html)
- Built-in `Connector`
- [indexing](https://docs.rs/indexing/index.html)
- Background / incremental indexing (feature gap Phase 11).
- [pipeline](https://docs.rs/pipeline/index.html)
- The ingestion pipeline: pull → chunk → embed → store (feature gap G1).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Deterministic](https://docs.rs/struct.DeterministicEmbedder.html)- Embedder
- Deterministic, network-free pseudo-embedder.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Input](https://docs.rs/enum.InputType.html)- Type
- Whether an embedding is for a document being stored or a search query.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_EMBEDDING_DIM.html)- EMBEDDING_ - DIM
- Default embedding dimension (Voyage `voyage-3-large`shape; mirrors smooai’s`knowledge_vectors embedding vector(1024)`).

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Embedder](https://docs.rs/trait.Embedder.html)
- Turn text into dense vectors. Implementations must return one vector per
input string, each of length `Embedder::dim`

# smooth_operator - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator/1.11.1/smooth_operator/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#smooth-operator)smooth-operator

The reference core for smooth-operator — the service layer on top of
[ smooth_operator_core](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-core/0.15.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator_core/index.html) (the agent engine). It defines three things:

- `domain`- `spec/domain/*.json`. Checkpoints re-use the engine’s- `smooth_operator_core::Checkpoint`
- `adapter`- `StorageAdapter`- `docs/STORAGE.md`). Its checkpoint/knowledge accessors return smooth-operator-core’s own traits so the engine plugs straight in.
- `runtime`- `AgentRuntime`- `Agent`- `Workflow`

It also owns two shared retrieval seams both backends/consumers depend on:
[ embedding](https://docs.rs/embedding/index.html) (the text→vector

[+ the network-free](https://docs.rs/embedding/trait.Embedder.html)

`Embedder`[, the one home for both the Postgres adapter and the ingestion pipeline) and](https://docs.rs/embedding/struct.DeterministicEmbedder.html)

`DeterministicEmbedder`[(the optional post-retrieval](https://docs.rs/rerank/index.html)

`rerank`[stage — feature gap G8).](https://docs.rs/rerank/trait.Reranker.html)

`Reranker`## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [access_](https://docs.rs/access_control/index.html)- control
- Document-level access control (feature gap G3).
- [adapter](https://docs.rs/adapter/index.html)
- The `StorageAdapter`seam.
- [agent_](https://docs.rs/agent_config/index.html)- config
- Per-agent behavior config (SMOODEV-590 parity in Rust).
- [auth](https://docs.rs/auth/index.html)
- Authentication + role-based access control (Phase 12).
- [backplane](https://docs.rs/backplane/index.html)
- Connection backplane: the scale-out + event-delivery seam for the WebSocket server.
- [connector_](https://docs.rs/connector_config/index.html)- config
- Connector configuration storage (Phase 12, increment 3).
- [curation](https://docs.rs/curation/index.html)
- Document sets, curation boosting, and query-time metadata filters (feature gap, Phase 11 — “Document sets / curation / boosting”).
- [domain](https://docs.rs/domain/index.html)
- Domain model for smooth-operator.
- [embedding](https://docs.rs/embedding/index.html)
- Text → vector embedding — the shared seam for dense retrieval.
- [gateway_](https://docs.rs/gateway_key/index.html)- key
- Per-org LLM gateway-key resolution: the seam that lets a multi-tenant
deployment bill/scope each org’s turns to its **own**gateway key while a standalone/local server keeps using the single environment key.
- [otp](https://docs.rs/otp/index.html)
- End-user identity verification (OTP) — the seam that lets a host wire a
one-time-code flow behind a public agent’s `end_user`tool auth, while the reference server stays credential-free.
- [rerank](https://docs.rs/rerank/index.html)
- Reranking — the optional post-retrieval reorder stage (feature gap G8).
- [runtime](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html)
- Minimal `AgentRuntime`that proves smooth-operator consumes smooth-operator.
- [settings](https://docs.rs/settings/index.html)
- Per-org agent settings storage (Phase 12, increment 3).
- [telemetry](https://docs.rs/telemetry/index.html)
- OpenTelemetry GenAI instrumentation for the agent turn.
- [tool_](https://docs.rs/tool_provider/index.html)- provider
- Host-contributed tool injection seam.
- [tools](https://docs.rs/tools/index.html)
- Tools the smooth-operator runtime registers on the smooth-operator-core engine.
- [widget_](https://docs.rs/widget_auth/index.html)- auth
- Embeddable-widget auth: an origin allowlist + public-key `authContext`verification for browser-embedded chat widgets (`<smooth-agent-chat>`).

- [Checkpoint](https://docs.rs/struct.Checkpoint.html)
- A checkpoint captures the full state of an agent at a point in time.

# stop - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/stop-cli/0.0.2/stop/

## Expand description

Process and system monitoring with structured output.

Provides cross-platform system metrics collection with filtering, sorting, and multiple output formats (JSON, CSV, human-readable).

- [SetPsm](https://docs.rs/struct.SetPsmStorageVersionV2.html)- Storage - Version - V2
- One-shot migration: writes `pallet_psm`’s on-chain storage version to v2. Required because`RemovePallet<PsmName>`(above in the migration tuple) wipes the pallet’s`:__STORAGE_VERSION__:`key, and`InitializePsm`doesn’t re-seed it. Without this, try-runtime’s post-upgrade check sees in-code = 2, on-chain = 0 and panics.

# masl_formatter - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/masl_formatter/1.0.0/masl_formatter/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#masl_formatter)masl_formatter

Canonical source code formatter for `.mdk` files.

Consumes an `masl_ast::Document` and produces formatted MASL source text.
Never modifies semantics. Guarantees idempotency: fmt(fmt(S)) == fmt(S).

See RFC-0019 — Formatter.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [format](https://docs.rs/fn.format.html)
- Format a parsed AST Document back to canonical MASL source text.

- [Connection](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html)
- A single QUIC connection.
- [Connection](https://docs.rs/struct.ConnectionRef.html)- Ref
- Same as the owned type but does not own the handle. Only used in callback wrapping where handle should not be closed by default.
- [Connection](https://docs.rs/struct.ConnectionShutdownFlags.html)- Shutdown - Flags
- Controls connection shutdown behavior.
- [Credential](https://docs.rs/struct.CredentialConfig.html)- Config
- [Credential](https://docs.rs/struct.CredentialFlags.html)- Flags
- Modifies the default credential configuration.
- [Handshake](https://docs.rs/struct.HandshakeInfo.html)- Info
- [Listener](https://docs.rs/struct.Listener.html)
- A single server listener
- [Listener](https://docs.rs/struct.ListenerRef.html)- Ref
- Same as the owned type but does not own the handle. Only used in callback wrapping where handle should not be closed by default.
- [NewConnection](https://docs.rs/struct.NewConnectionInfo.html)- Info
- [Quic](https://docs.rs/struct.QuicListenerStatistics.html)- Listener - Statistics
- A helper struct for accessing listener statistics.

- A helper struct for accessing performance counters.

- [Receive](https://docs.rs/struct.ReceiveFlags.html)- Flags
- [Registration](https://docs.rs/struct.Registration.html)
- The execution context for processing connections on the application’s behalf.

- Specifies the configuration for a new registration.

- Controls stream and datagram send behavior.
- [Settings](https://docs.rs/struct.Settings.html)
- Settings for MsQuic Wrapping QUIC_SETTINGS ffi type.
- [Status](https://docs.rs/struct.Status.html)
- Quic status used in non-ffi code. Internal representation matches the os platfrom type. Used for all non-ffi error return and callback status code fields.

- Stream callback. msquic never executes stream callback on the same stream in parallel.

# bridge_hub_test_utils - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bridge-hub-test-utils/0.34.0/bridge_hub_test_utils/

## Expand description

Module contains predefined test-case scenarios for “BridgeHub” `Runtime`s.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [test_](https://docs.rs/test_cases/index.html)- cases
- Module contains predefined test-case scenarios for `Runtime`with bridging capabilities.
- [test_](https://docs.rs/test_data/index.html)- data
- Generating test data, used by all tests.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Collator](https://docs.rs/struct.CollatorSessionKey.html)- Session - Key
- [Collator](https://docs.rs/struct.CollatorSessionKeys.html)- Session - Keys
- [ExtBuilder](https://docs.rs/struct.ExtBuilder.html)
- Basic builder based on balances, collators and pallet_session.

- [Slot](https://docs.rs/struct.SlotDurations.html)- Durations

- Enum representing governance origin/location.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Basic](https://docs.rs/trait.BasicParachainRuntime.html)- Parachain - Runtime
- A set of traits for a minimal parachain runtime, that may be used in conjunction with the
`ExtBuilder`and the`RuntimeHelper`.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [assert_](https://docs.rs/fn.assert_metadata.html)- metadata
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/fn.assert_total.html)- total
- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_sane_fees_values.html)- sane_ - fees_ - values
- A helper function for comparing the actual value of a fee constant with its estimated value. The
estimated value can be overestimated (`overestimate_in_percent`), and if the difference to the actual value is below`margin_overestimate_diff_in_percent_for_lowering`, we should lower the actual value.
- [diff_](https://docs.rs/fn.diff_as_percent.html)- as_ - percent
- [ensure_](https://docs.rs/fn.ensure_opened_bridge.html)- opened_ - bridge
- Helper function to open the bridge/lane for `source`and`destination`while ensuring all required balances are placed into the SA of the source.
- [mock_](https://docs.rs/fn.mock_open_hrmp_channel.html)- open_ - hrmp_ - channel
- Helper function which emulates opening HRMP channel which is needed for `XcmpQueue`to pass.
- [open_](https://docs.rs/fn.open_bridge_with_extrinsic.html)- bridge_ - with_ - extrinsic
- Utility for opening bridge with dedicated `pallet_xcm_bridge_hub`’s extrinsic.
- [open_](https://docs.rs/fn.open_bridge_with_storage.html)- bridge_ - with_ - storage
- Utility for opening bridge directly inserting data to the `pallet_xcm_bridge_hub`’s storage (used only for legacy purposes).
- [test_](https://docs.rs/fn.test_header.html)- header
- Get a header for testing.

# aipmc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/aipmc/0.0.1/aipmc/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#aipmc-aip-%E6%99%BA%E8%83%BD%E4%BD%93%E4%BA%92%E8%81%94%E5%8D%8F%E8%AE%AE-mcu-%E5%AE%9E%E7%8E%B0)aipmc: AIP 智能体互联协议 MCU 实现

本 crate 是 AIPMC 项目的统一导出层，将所有子模块重新导出，
用户只需引入 `aipmc` 即可使用完整的协议栈功能。

[§](https://docs.rs#%E5%AD%90%E6%A8%A1%E5%9D%97)子模块

| 模块 | crate | 说明 |
|---|---|---|
| `basic` | aipmc-basic | 核心协议库（协议/消息/编解码） |
| `transport` | aipmc-transport | 传输层（UART/WiFi/BLE） |
| [ `esp32`] | aipmc-esp32 | ESP-32 平台适配（需 feature） |
| [ `stm32`] | aipmc-stm32 | STM-32 平台适配（需 feature） |

[§](https://docs.rs#%E4%BD%BF%E7%94%A8%E7%A4%BA%E4%BE%8B)使用示例

```
use aipmc::basic::{AgentCard, AgentSkill, AcpMessage, AcpMethod, AgentCapability};
let agent = AgentCard::new("dev-01", "MyAgent", "A test agent")
    .unwrap()
    .with_capability(AgentCapability::SensorRead)
    .unwrap()
    .with_skill(AgentSkill::new("temp", "ReadTemp", "Read temperature").unwrap())
    .unwrap();
let msg = AcpMessage::with_payload(AcpMethod::Initialize, 0, b"hello").unwrap();
let encoded = msg.encode().unwrap();
let decoded = AcpMessage::decode(&encoded).unwrap();
assert_eq!(decoded.session_id, 0);
```

---

# aipmc_stm32 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/aipmc-stm32/0.0.1/aipmc_stm32/

[§](#aipmc-stm32-aip-%E6%99%BA%E8%83%BD%E4%BD%93%E4%BA%92%E8%81%94%E5%8D%8F%E8%AE%AE-stm-32-%E5%B9%B3%E5%8F%B0%E9%80%82%E9%85%8D%E5%B1%82)aipmc-stm32: AIP 智能体互联协议 STM-32 平台适配层

提供 STM-32 系列芯片的硬件抽象层（HAL），封装 UART/SPI 初始化、
GPIO 控制等平台特定功能，使上层协议栈无需关注硬件细节。

[§](#%E6%94%AF%E6%8C%81%E7%9A%84%E8%8A%AF%E7%89%87%E7%B3%BB%E5%88%97)支持的芯片系列

| Feature | 芯片系列 |
|---|
| `stm32f4` | STM32F4xx |
| `stm32h7` | STM32H7xx |
| `stm32l4` | STM32L4xx |
| `stm32g4` | STM32G4xx |

[§](#%E5%BD%93%E5%89%8D%E7%8A%B6%E6%80%81)当前状态

骨架实现，待对接 `stm32-hal` 后完善。

---

# cidr 0.3.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cidr/0.3.2

# cidr crate

This library provides types to represent an IP network (`Cidr`) or an IP
host within a network (`Inet`).

The naming follows the names of the [PostgreSQL data types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/static/datatype-net-types.html)

The documentation for `master` is located at [https://stbuehler.github.io/rustdocs/cidr/cidr/](https://stbuehler.github.io/rustdocs/cidr/cidr/); released versions are documented at [https://docs.rs/cidr](https://docs.rs/cidr).

## Examples

- example making good use of the `bitstring`feature and the`bitstring-trees`crate:[https://github.com/stbuehler/rust-gather-cidr-map](https://github.com/stbuehler/rust-gather-cidr-map)

---

# cidr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cidr/0.3.2/target-redirect/cidr/

## Expand description

This library provides types to represent an IP network ([ Cidr](https://docs.rs/trait.Cidr.html)) or
an IP host withing a network (

[)](https://docs.rs/trait.Inet.html)

`Inet`The naming follows the names of the [PostgreSQL data types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/static/datatype-net-types.html)

By default address parsing is done using `FromStr` from the standard
library, which is rather strict in the inputs it accepts.
[ Cidr](https://docs.rs/trait.Cidr.html) types don’t accept addresses with host-bits set (i.e.

`127.0.0.1/8`
isn’t valid; it should be `127.0.0.0/8`).Custom parsing can be implemented using the helpers in the [ parsers](https://docs.rs/parsers/index.html) module.

If the `#` flag is used with the `Display` formatting (i.e. `{:#}`) the
prefix length will be shown even for host addresses (added in `0.1.1`).

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-no_unsafe)Feature `no_unsafe`

Enables `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` for the whole crate; needs to use
some workarounds that are likely slower than their `unsafe` variants.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-std)Feature `std`

Enabled by default, currently unused.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-serde)Feature `serde`

This feature enables various types to be serialized using `serde`
(without `serde-derive`).

In human readable formats the `Display` and `FromStr` interfaces are
used.  Otherwise all values are serialized in the same format (apart
from the newtype wrapping) as a tuple of two values:

- `tag: u8`:- `0x00...0x20`: IPv4 with network length- `tag`
- `0x40...0xc0`: IPv6 with network length- `tag - 0x40`
- `0xff`:- `any`

- address according to `tag`:`Ipv4Addr``[u8; 4]`),`Ipv6Addr``[u8; 16]`) or`()`

The represenation hasn’t been changed in 0.2; it is compatible with 0.1.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-bitstring)Feature `bitstring`

This feature allows various types to be used as [ bitstring::BitString](https://docs.rs/bitstring/0.2.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/bitstring/bit_string/trait.BitString.html),
which allows them being in used in containers like

[bitstring-trees](https://crates.io/crates/bitstring-trees).

## Expand description

This library provides types to represent an IP network ([ Cidr](https://docs.rs/trait.Cidr.html)) or
an IP host withing a network (

[)](https://docs.rs/trait.Inet.html)

`Inet`The naming follows the names of the [PostgreSQL data types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/static/datatype-net-types.html)

library, which is rather strict in the inputs it accepts.
[ Cidr](https://docs.rs/trait.Cidr.html) types don’t accept addresses with host-bits set (i.e.

`127.0.0.1/8`
isn’t valid; it should be `127.0.0.0/8`).Custom parsing can be implemented using the helpers in the [ parsers](https://docs.rs/parsers/index.html) module.

If the `#` flag is used with the `Display` formatting (i.e. `{:#}`) the
prefix length will be shown even for host addresses (added in `0.1.1`).

some workarounds that are likely slower than their `unsafe` variants.

}## Expand description

Types implementing [ Cidr](https://docs.rs/trait.Cidr.html) represent IP networks.  An IP network in
this case is a set of IP addresses which share a common prefix (when
viewed as a bitstring).  The length of this prefix is called

`network_length`.In the standard representation the network is identified by the first address and the network length, separated by a ‘/’.

The parsers will expect the input in the same format, i.e. only the first address of the network is accepted.

The first network length bits in an address representing the network are the network part, the remaining bits are the host part. Requiring an address to be the first in a network is equivalent to requiring the host part being zero.

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Create new network from address and prefix length. If the network length exceeds the address length or the address is not the first address in the network (“host part not zero”) an error is returned.

Create a network containing a single address (network length = address length).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cidr/traits.rs.html#87)#### fn [iter](https://docs.rs#tymethod.iter)(&self) -> [InetIterator](https://docs.rs/struct.InetIterator.html)<Self::[Address](https://docs.rs/trait.Cidr.html#associatedtype.Address)> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cidr/traits.rs.html#87)

#### fn [iter](https://docs.rs#tymethod.iter)(&self) -> [InetIterator](https://docs.rs/struct.InetIterator.html)<Self::[Address](https://docs.rs/trait.Cidr.html#associatedtype.Address)> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

Iterate over all addresses in the range.  With IPv6 addresses
this can produce really long iterations (up to 2128
addresses).

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

}## Expand description

Types implementing Inet represent IP hosts within networks.

In addition to the network represented by the corresponding [ Cidr](https://docs.rs/trait.Cidr.html)
type, an

[type also stores a single host address which is part of the network.](https://docs.rs/trait.Inet.html)

`Inet`The host address is not really stored as separate data, but is stored together with the network address.

The representation of a [ Inet](https://docs.rs/trait.Inet.html) type is similar to that of the
corresponding

[type, but uses the host address instead of the first address of the network.](https://docs.rs/trait.Cidr.html)

`Cidr`## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Create new host within a network from address and prefix length. If the network length exceeds the address length an error is returned.

Create a network containing a single address as host and the network (network length = address length).

increments host part (without changing the network part); returns true on wrap around

Returns next address in network or `None` if it was the last address in the network

decrements host part (without changing the network part); returns true on wrap around

Returns previous address in network or `None` if it was the first address in the network

# cidr::parsers - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cidr/0.3.2/cidr/parsers/index.html

## Expand description

Extra parsers

The `FromStr` implementations in this crate are rather strict
about the allowed input.  Depending on the data format that needs
to be handled the functions here might help implementing custom
parsers.

The parser combinators that take an `address_parser` can either
take `FromStr::from_str` or a non-default parser like [ parse_loose_ip](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_loose_ip.html).
They are used to parse addresses (either as part of a

`"/"` separated
notation or as single host).Parser combinators that take an additional `host_parser` use that
to parse strings that don’t have an `"/"` separator - usually these
should return Cidr/Inet “host” values, but they can allow special
syntax like [ parse_short_ip_cidr](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_short_ip_cidr.html) to represent non-host networks too.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [inet_](https://docs.rs/fn.inet_addr.html)- addr
- Parse “loose” IPv4 address similar to POSIX `inet_addr`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_any_cidr.html)- any_ - cidr
- Parse `AnyIpCidr`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_any_cidr_full.html)- any_ - cidr_ - full
- Parse `AnyIpCidr`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_any_cidr_full_ignore_hostbits.html)- any_ - cidr_ - full_ - ignore_ - hostbits
- Parse `AnyIpCidr`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_any_cidr_ignore_hostbits.html)- any_ - cidr_ - ignore_ - hostbits
- Parse `AnyIpCidr`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_cidr.html)- cidr
- Parse `Cidr`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_cidr_full.html)- cidr_ - full
- Parse `Cidr`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_cidr_full_ignore_hostbits.html)- cidr_ - full_ - ignore_ - hostbits
- Parse `Cidr`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_cidr_ignore_hostbits.html)- cidr_ - ignore_ - hostbits
- Parse `Cidr`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_inet.html)- inet
- Parse `Inet`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_inet_full.html)- inet_ - full
- Parse `Inet`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_loose_ip.html)- loose_ - ip
- Parse IP address; fall back to `inet_addr`if normal parser fails
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_loose_ipv4.html)- loose_ - ipv4
- Parse IPv4 address; fall back to `inet_addr`if normal parser fails
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_short_any_ip_cidr.html)- short_ - any_ - ip_ - cidr
- Parses normal IP CIDR notations, `"any"`or short IPv4 forms via`parse_short_ipv4_address_as_cidr`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_short_ip_address_as_cidr.html)- short_ - ip_ - address_ - as_ - cidr
- Parses normal IP addresses as host addresses, and short IPv4 addresses via `parse_short_ipv4_address_as_cidr`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_short_ip_cidr.html)- short_ - ip_ - cidr
- Parses normal IP CIDR notations or short IPv4 forms via `parse_short_ipv4_address_as_cidr`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_short_ipv4_address_as_cidr.html)- short_ - ipv4_ - address_ - as_ - cidr
- Parse “short” IPv4 addresses as networks with octet-aligned length
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_short_ipv4_cidr.html)- short_ - ipv4_ - cidr
- Parses normal IPv4 CIDR notations or short forms via `parse_short_ipv4_address_as_cidr`

# cidr::errors - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cidr/0.3.2/cidr/errors/index.html

## Expand description

Various error types returned by function in this crate

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Network](https://docs.rs/struct.NetworkLengthTooLongError.html)- Length - TooLong - Error
- Error returned when the network length was longer than the address

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Inet](https://docs.rs/enum.InetTupleError.html)- Tuple - Error
- Error type returned when creating `Inet`
- [Network](https://docs.rs/enum.NetworkParseError.html)- Parse - Error
- Error type returned when parsing IP networks

Create new network from address and prefix length. If the network length exceeds the address length or the address is not the first address in the network (“host part not zero”) an error is returned.

# Ipv4Inet in cidr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cidr/0.3.2/cidr/struct.Ipv4Inet.html

`pub struct Ipv4Inet { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Create new host within a network from address and prefix length. If the network length exceeds the address length an error is returned.

Create a network containing a single address as host and the network (network length = address length).

increments host part (without changing the network part); returns true on wrap around

Returns next address in network or `None` if it was the last address in the network

decrements host part (without changing the network part); returns true on wrap around

Returns previous address in network or `None` if it was the first address in the network

# Ipv6Inet in cidr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cidr/0.3.2/cidr/struct.Ipv6Inet.html

`pub struct Ipv6Inet { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Create new host within a network from address and prefix length. If the network length exceeds the address length an error is returned.

Create a network containing a single address as host and the network (network length = address length).

increments host part (without changing the network part); returns true on wrap around

Returns next address in network or `None` if it was the last address in the network

decrements host part (without changing the network part); returns true on wrap around

Returns previous address in network or `None` if it was the first address in the network

# AnyIpCidr in cidr - Rust

Enum AnyIpCidr   Copy item path  Source  ```
pub enum AnyIpCidr {
    Any,
    V4(
```
Ipv4Cidr ),
    V6(Ipv6Cidr ),
}Expand description Represents either an IPv4 or an IPv6 network or “any”.

Allows for a bit string representation which treats “any” as the
empty string, IPv4 as starting with `false` and IPv6 as starting
with `true`. After the first bit the normal represenation for the
picked address-family follows.

Setting the first bit (using the `bitstring` API) always truncates
the bit string to length 1 (i.e. `/0` in the resulting family).

The `Cidr`

“any” network containing all IPv4 and IPv6 addresses

Whether representing any address

Whether representing an IPv4 network

Whether representing an IPv6 network

network length exceeds the address length or the address is not
the first address in the network (“host part not zero”) an error
is returned.

Create a network containing a single address (network length =
address length).

first address in the network as plain address

returns `None``Any`

# cidr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cidr/latest/cidr/

## Expand description

This library provides types to represent an IP network ([ Cidr](https://docs.rs/trait.Cidr.html)) or
an IP host withing a network (

[)](https://docs.rs/trait.Inet.html)

`Inet`The naming follows the names of the [PostgreSQL data types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/static/datatype-net-types.html)

By default address parsing is done using `FromStr` from the standard
library, which is rather strict in the inputs it accepts.
[ Cidr](https://docs.rs/trait.Cidr.html) types don’t accept addresses with host-bits set (i.e.

`127.0.0.1/8`
isn’t valid; it should be `127.0.0.0/8`).Custom parsing can be implemented using the helpers in the [ parsers](https://docs.rs/parsers/index.html) module.

If the `#` flag is used with the `Display` formatting (i.e. `{:#}`) the
prefix length will be shown even for host addresses (added in `0.1.1`).

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-no_unsafe)Feature `no_unsafe`

Enables `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` for the whole crate; needs to use
some workarounds that are likely slower than their `unsafe` variants.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-std)Feature `std`

Enabled by default, currently unused.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-serde)Feature `serde`

This feature enables various types to be serialized using `serde`
(without `serde-derive`).

In human readable formats the `Display` and `FromStr` interfaces are
used.  Otherwise all values are serialized in the same format (apart
from the newtype wrapping) as a tuple of two values:

- `tag: u8`:- `0x00...0x20`: IPv4 with network length- `tag`
- `0x40...0xc0`: IPv6 with network length- `tag - 0x40`
- `0xff`:- `any`

- address according to `tag`:`Ipv4Addr``[u8; 4]`),`Ipv6Addr``[u8; 16]`) or`()`

The represenation hasn’t been changed in 0.2; it is compatible with 0.1.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-bitstring)Feature `bitstring`

This feature allows various types to be used as [ bitstring::BitString](https://docs.rs/bitstring/0.2.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/bitstring/bit_string/trait.BitString.html),
which allows them being in used in containers like

[bitstring-trees](https://crates.io/crates/bitstring-trees).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

# bincode 1.3.3 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/bincode/^1.3.1

# Bincode

A compact encoder / decoder pair that uses a binary zero-fluff encoding scheme. The size of the encoded object will be the same or smaller than the size that the object takes up in memory in a running Rust program.

In addition to exposing two simple functions
(one that encodes to `Vec<u8>`, and one that decodes from `&[u8]`),
binary-encode exposes a Reader/Writer API that makes it work
perfectly with other stream-based APIs such as Rust files, network streams,
and the [flate2-rs](https://github.com/alexcrichton/flate2-rs) compression
library.

## Bincode in the wild

- [google/tarpc](https://github.com/google/tarpc): Bincode is used to serialize and deserialize networked RPC messages.
- [servo/webrender](https://github.com/servo/webrender): Bincode records webrender API calls for record/replay-style graphics debugging.
- [servo/ipc-channel](https://github.com/servo/ipc-channel): IPC-Channel uses Bincode to send structs between processes using a channel-like API.

## Example

```
use ;
;
```
## Details

The encoding (and thus decoding) proceeds unsurprisingly -- primitive
types are encoded according to the underlying `Writer`, tuples and
structs are encoded by encoding their fields one-by-one, and enums are
encoded by first writing out the tag representing the variant and
then the contents.

However, there are some implementation details to be aware of:

- `isize`/- `usize`are encoded as- `i64`/- `u64`, for portability.
- enums variants are encoded as a `u32`instead of a`usize`.`u32`is enough for all practical uses.
- `str`is encoded as- `(u64, &[u8])`, where the- `u64`is the number of bytes contained in the encoded string.

## Specification

Bincode's format will eventually be codified into a specification, along with its configuration options and default configuration. In the meantime, here are some frequently asked questions regarding use of the crate:

### Is Bincode suitable for storage?

The encoding format is stable across minor revisions, provided the same configuration is used. This should ensure that later versions can still read data produced by a previous versions of the library if no major version change has occured.

Bincode is invariant over byte-order in the default configuration
(`bincode::options::DefaultOptions`), making an exchange between different
architectures possible. It is also rather space efficient, as it stores no
metadata like struct field names in the output format and writes long streams of
binary data without needing any potentially size-increasing encoding.

As a result, Bincode is suitable for storing data. Be aware that it does not implement any sort of data versioning scheme or file headers, as these features are outside the scope of this crate.

### Is Bincode suitable for untrusted inputs?

Bincode attempts to protect against hostile data. There is a maximum size
configuration available (`bincode::config::Bounded`), but not enabled in the
default configuration. Enabling it causes pre-allocation size to be limited to
prevent against memory exhaustion attacks.

Deserializing any incoming data will not cause undefined behavior or memory issues, assuming that the deserialization code for the struct is safe itself.

Bincode can be used for untrusted inputs in the sense that it will not create a security issues in your application, provided the configuration is changed to enable a maximum size limit. Malicious inputs will fail upon deserialization.

### What is Bincode's MSRV (minimum supported Rust version)?

Bincode 1.0 maintains support for rust 1.18.0. Any changes to this are considered a breaking change for semver purposes.

---

# serde_test 1.0.177 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/serde_test/^1.0.27

This crate provides a convenient concise way to write unit tests for
implementations of [ Serialize](serde::ser::Serialize) and

[.](serde::de::Deserialize)

`Deserialize`The `Serialize` impl for a value can be characterized by the sequence of
[ Serializer](serde::ser::Serializer) calls that are made in the course of serializing the value, so

`serde_test` provides a [`Token`] abstraction which corresponds roughly to
`Serializer` method calls. There is an [`assert_ser_tokens`] function to test
that a value serializes to a particular sequence of method calls, an
[`assert_de_tokens`] function to test that a value can be deserialized from a
particular sequence of method calls, and an [`assert_tokens`] function to test
both directions. There are also functions to test expected failure conditions.Here is an example from the [ linked-hash-map](https://github.com/contain-rs/linked-hash-map) crate.

```
use LinkedHashMap;
use ;
```
